title: Structured Choice in Group-Heavy Mechanical Engineering Laboratories: Student Reflections on Autonomy, Collaboration, and Participation Norms
content: This paper examines how undergraduate engineering students describe collaboration, autonomy, and participation in a laboratory learning environment. Using de-identified responses from an end-of-term self-reflection survey (50 valid closed-ended responses), the study analyzes items on productive work arrangements, preferred lab formats, approaches to complex technical problems, question-asking, learning preferences, comfort in group settings, perceived disadvantage, and course redesign priorities. The results show a productive tension. Students strongly valued structured in-person laboratory learning, small-team work, hands-on experimentation, and accessible help-seeking. At the same time, 40.0% reported that their preferred learning style had placed them at a disadvantage at least occasionally, and 52.0% believed that students who prefer working alone are probably or definitely disadvantaged in group-heavy engineering curricula. The paper argues that inclusive engineering pedagogy should not ask instructors to choose between teamwork and individual autonomy. Instead, it proposes structured choice: small, purposeful teams combined with individual sense-making time, explicit role design, normalized question-asking, authentic engineering cases, and multiple routes for demonstrating contribution. The findings offer a compact pedagogical framework for making group-heavy laboratory education more inclusive without weakening hands-on rigor or collaborative professional preparation.
